It seems that the government, or at least Mr. Churchill, intended this limb of the definition to cover everything to do with taxation and, in particular, to cover all aspects of administration by the phrase “the regulation of taxation”[footnote 4]

1.12. In the case of the 1976 Finance Bill the inclusion of Schedule 6, which gave tax inspectors powers to demand information and search premises, did not prevent the certification of the Bill as a Money Bill. These provisions provoked complaints in the Lords that this was “tacking” within what is now Lords Standing Order No. 51 but the allegation was not upheld by the Practice and Procedure Committee to which it was referred[footnote 5].

1.13. However, the inclusion of provisions about administration might result in a Bill not being certified as a Money Bill.

1.14. Erskine May[footnote 6] notes that the Tax Credits Bill in the 2001-02 session was not certified on the basis that, although it established two new tax credits, it also made changes to the administration of child benefit and guardian’s allowance.

1.15. Bills will be certified if they are otherwise within the definition even though their objects are not purely fiscal, or indeed not fiscal at all. This applies whether the ulterior object is to be gathered from the government’s explanation of the Bill, as in the case of the Selective Employment Payments Bill 1966, or whether it appears on the face of the Bill, as with various anti-dumping and similar duties (for example, those provided for in the Safeguarding of Industries Bill 1921 or the Abnormal Importations (Customs Duties) Bill 1932).

“Imposition for the payment of debt or other financial purposes of charges on the Consolidated Fund, the National Loans Fund or on money provided by Parliament, or the variation or repeal of any such charges”

1.16. The qualifying words “for the payment of debt or other financial purposes” require a clear distinction, when a provision is imposing, varying or repealing a charge, between the case where the primary purpose of the provision is to impose, vary or repeal the charge (i.e. a financial purpose), and the case where the provision is for some other primary purpose (usually social or economic).

1.17. Whether the primary purpose is financial should be determined primarily from the text of the Bill. Ministerial statements may be informative, but are likely to be dealing with the effects of the measures (with all spending and taxation measures having non-financial effects); and one should not read purpose back from effects.

1.18. A Bill that creates a simple grant scheme (i.e. a scheme that is confined to imposing or varying charges on public funds) is likely to be certified. An example is the Bill for the Childcare Payments Act 2014.

1.19. The more complex a scheme is, however, the more likely it is that either the Bill will contain other non-subordinate provisions which create a basis for non-certification or that the primary purpose of the scheme may be interpreted as not being financial (and there may well be an interaction between the two).

1.20. Examples of Bills that were not certified and can be understood in this light are the Bills that became the Family Allowances Act 1945, the Reinsurance (Acts of Terrorism) Act 1993, the Tax Credits Act 2002, the Child Trust Funds Act 2004 and the Saving Gateways Act 2009. The sorts of provisions that may have rendered these Bills uncertifiable include provisions regarding interactions with contributory benefits, payments by private parties, and the creation of financial services products.

1.21. Where a Bill amends or repeals a charge imposed by an earlier Act, the fact that the Act was not certified is not conclusive as to the certifiability of the Bill. The certifiability of the Bill will depend on whether the purpose of the amendment or repeal is financial. As a result, the distinction between complex and simple grant schemes applies only to their creation: any subsequent variation to a scheme can be considered in isolation.

1.22. An example of the general principle described in paragraph 1.21 was the Bill that became the Savings Account and Health in Pregnancy Grant Act 201. This Bill removed eligibility for a child trust fund (by amending the Child Trust Funds Act 2004) and entitlement to health in pregnancy gran[footnote 7] and repealed the whole of the Saving Gateway Accounts Act 2009. The purpose of the Bill was to repeal charges on the Consolidated Fund, meaning that it was certified as a Money Bill despite the non-certification of the earlier Acts.

1.23. Authorising expenditure is a financial purpose. Therefore, pure “Baldwin Agreement Bills” are typically certified as Money Bills if they are confined to authorising expenditure. Examples are the Rolls-Royce (Purchase) Bill 1971, the Job Release Bill 1977, the High Speed Rail (Preparation) Bill 2013 and the Windrush Compensation Scheme (Expenditure) Bill in the 2019-21 Session. Baldwin Agreement Bills are Bills necessary only in consequence of the agreement in 1932-4 between the Public Accounts Committee and the Treasury that significant items of government expenditure running for more than one financial year should be authorised by a specific Act and not merely by the Appropriation Act each year.

“Imposition of charges on the Consolidated Fund, the National Loans Fund or on money provided by Parliament”

1.24. If a Bill provides for the imposition of charges partly on the Consolidated Fund, the National Loans Fund or money provided by Parliament and partly on the National Insurance Fund, the Bill will not be a Money Bill. For example, a Bill that (for a financial purpose) increases expenditure under section 150A of the Social Security Administration Act 1992 will not be a Money Bill because, whilst some of the benefits mentioned in that section are payable out of money provided by Parliament, others are payable out of the National Insurance Fund.

1.60. There was some discussion in Parliament when the Parliament Bill was being debated as to whether section 1(1) requires the Bill to be presented for Royal Assent immediately the month is up[footnote 22]. The view put forward in answer by Sir Herbert Samuel was that the section imposes an obligation to present for Royal Assent but does not specify when this is to be done. The timing of the issuing of a commission for giving Royal Assent is a matter for His Majesty’s Ministers to advise on, that is to say the government fixes the date. The general rule is that when a commission is prepared all Bills should be inserted which are then waiting for Royal Assent or which are likely to have passed by the time Royal Assent is to be declared[footnote 23].

(a) Finance Bills which are often, but not always, certified, and

(b) Consolidated Fund and Appropriation Bills, now Supply and Appropriation Bills, which are always certified.

(It also excludes Isle of Man (Customs) Bills, which appear usually to have been certified and are no longer passed at Westminster as Tynwald has power to legislate.)

In recent sessions (2017-19, 2019 and 2022-23) there have been Northern Ireland Budget Bills that have been certified as Money Bills. They provided for the appropriation of money out of the Northern Ireland Consolidated Fund for the then current financial year; normally such a Bill would be taken through the Northern Ireland Assembly. The sums referred to in the Bills were derived from sums voted out of the UK Consolidated Fund into the Northern Ireland Consolidated Fund by a UK Supply and Appropriation (Main Estimates) Act, together with revenue generated within Northern Ireland. Two Northern Ireland Budget (Anticipation and Adjustments) Bills were also certified in the 2017-19 Session. ↩
